    - heading "Where does our sign-in stand?" [level=1]
    - generic: "Date: 1 November 2026"
    - generic: "Sources checked: 19 October 2026; corrected points 23 October 2026"
    - generic: At least one of the three first steps is open.
    - paragraph: Step 1 done, step 2 open, step 3 done. The three steps are what the authorities cited below recommend first and what security questionnaires from customers and insurers ask about.
    - heading "What you told us" [level=2]
    - term: MFA on email
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: MFA on admin and remote access
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: Second factor
    - definition: A security key or a passkey
    - term: Password manager
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: Shared accounts
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: Password rules
    - definition: Long passwords, at least 12 to 15 characters, changed only when there is a suspicion
    - term: Leavers
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: Recovery
    - definition: "Yes"
    - heading "Where you stand" [level=2]
    - text: "Step 1: a second factor on every account that matters"
    - generic: Email, admin and remote access are covered with an app or a security key.
    - generic: Done
    - text: "Step 2: one long password per account, kept by a password manager"
    - generic: Shared logins, or neither a password manager nor a length rule.
    - generic: Open
    - text: "Step 3: one account per person, leavers off the same day, recovery tested"
    - generic: List of accounts, same-day offboarding, recovery codes offline.
    - generic: Done
    - heading "Findings" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: "The US standards body NIST published revision 4 of its Digital Identity Guidelines in July 2025; it supersedes revision 3. For passwords it requires: a minimum of 15 characters where the password is the only factor, and at least 8 characters where it is part of multi-factor authentication; no other composition rules such as required mixtures of character types; no periodic change, but a forced change where there is evidence of compromise; a check of every new password against a blocklist of commonly used, expected or compromised passwords; and that password managers and autofill are allowed; it recommends allowing paste. Failed attempts are rate-limited."
    - generic: "→ NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, July 2025, sections 3.1.1.1, 3.1.1.2 and 3.2.2 · pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html · retrieved 2026-10-19, section 3.1.1.2 · retrieved 2026-10-23"
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: "The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) writes that the advice to change passwords regularly is outdated: regular changes without a reason lead to weaker passwords, and employers should neither demand nor technically enforce them. A password is changed when there is a suspicion that it has leaked. Instead the BSI recommends strong passwords, a second factor or passkeys, and a password manager. Its IT-Grundschutz module ORP.4 requires that every user identifier can be attributed to one person, that unneeded identifiers and permissions are removed on personnel changes, that a password is never used for more than one system, that systems ask for a change only with a valid reason and avoid purely time-driven changes, and that a written copy exists only for an emergency and is kept securely."
    - generic: → BSI, press releases of 31 January 2025 ("Passwortwechseln war gestern") and 30 January 2026 ("Der Ändere-dein-Passwort-Tag braucht ein Update") · bsi.bund.de · retrieved 2026-10-19; BSI, IT-Grundschutz-Kompendium, module ORP.4 Identity and Access Management, requirements A1, A2, A8, A22, A23, and module ORP.2 Personnel, A2, edition 2023 · bsi.bund.de · retrieved 2026-10-19
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: "The US cybersecurity agency CISA ranks the forms of multi-factor authentication from strongest to weakest: phishing-resistant methods (FIDO/WebAuthn security keys and passkeys, PKI); app-based one-time codes, push notifications with number matching and hardware tokens; push notifications without number matching; and codes by SMS or voice call, which are vulnerable to phishing, SS7 and SIM-swap attacks and should be used only as a last resort. For small and medium businesses that cannot implement phishing-resistant MFA at once, CISA names app- or token-based codes and push with number matching as the best options. In June 2022 CISA's director said that multi-factor authentication can make you 99 % less likely to get hacked; a Microsoft study of real attack data found that it reduces the risk of compromise by 99.2 %."
    - generic: → CISA, fact sheet "Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA", October 2022, pp. 1 to 3 · cisa.gov · retrieved 2026-10-19; CISA, news release of 6 June 2022 and blog of 5 May 2022 · cisa.gov · retrieved 2026-10-19; Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2023 and Microsoft Research, "How effective is multifactor authentication at deterring cyberattacks?", May 2023 · microsoft.com · retrieved 2026-10-19
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: ENISA's guide for small and medium businesses encourages a passphrase of at least three random common words; for ordinary passwords it still suggests mixed character types, which NIST no longer requires. It asks never to reuse or share passwords, to enable multi-factor authentication, to use a dedicated password manager, to enforce strong passwords and where possible MFA for remote access, and to revoke an employee's access to business systems when they leave.
    - generic: "→ ENISA, \"Cybersecurity guide for SMEs: 12 steps to securing your business\", June 2021, steps 4 and 5 and the remote-access step (step 4 · retrieved 2026-10-23); ENISA, \"Cybersecurity for SMEs: Challenges and Recommendations\", June 2021, pp. 36 to 37 · enisa.europa.eu · retrieved 2026-10-19"
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: "The Austrian portal onlinesicherheit.gv.at recommends at least twelve characters for normal accounts and longer passwords or additional authentication for accounts with special rights, at least twenty characters for wireless networks and encrypted files, a change whenever there is a suspicion that a password became known to others, and password managers; it describes security keys as an effective measure against phishing and man-in-the-middle attacks. A WKO page of 2016 still online recommends eight characters and a change every three to six months; the WKO's own news of January 2026 says the opposite: length matters, at least twelve characters, change only on a concrete suspicion."
    - generic: "→ onlinesicherheit.gv.at (Federal Chancellery and A-SIT), \"Passwort-Auswahl\" (updated 9 December 2025), \"Passwort-Umgang\" (6 February 2020), news on FIDO security keys (19 September 2023) · retrieved 2026-10-19; WKO, \"Passwörter: Die Schlüssel zu Computer und Internet\", status 6 June 2016, and WKO Kärnten, \"Passwort vergessen, Konto gesperrt\", updated 28 January 2026 · wko.at · retrieved 2026-10-19"
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: For businesses covered by NIS 2, the measures must include basic cyber hygiene and cybersecurity training, access control policies, and the use of multi-factor or continuous authentication where appropriate. Germany and Austria wrote this wording into their laws.
    - generic: → Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Art. 21(2), points (g), (i) and (j) · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-19; BSI-Gesetz, § 30(2), no. 10 · gesetze-im-internet.de · retrieved 2026-10-19; NISG 2026, § 32(4), lit. j · ris.bka.gv.at · retrieved 2026-10-19
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Interpretation
      - text: A shared login cannot be attributed to a person, cannot bind a second factor to one phone, and keeps working after someone has left. Replace it with one account per person and delegated access to the shared mailbox or system; where a tool allows only one login, keep the password in the password manager with a named owner and change it at every departure.
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Gap
      - text: No source read gives a legal minimum for the sign-in security of a business outside NIS 2. The standards above are what the authorities recommend and what security questionnaires ask; a contract with a customer or an insurer may demand more.
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Uncertain
      - text: The BSI consumer pages carry no date; the IT-Grundschutz module read is from edition 2023, the latest full edition; the BSI is introducing IT-Grundschutz++ (to be checked at bsi.bund.de). CISA does not name the research behind its 99 % figure; the figure is reported as its statement, not as a measurement of this memo.
    - heading "What to do next" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem: Keep the second factor on every account that matters, and move any remaining SMS codes to an app or a security key.
      - listitem: Roll out a password manager for everyone; one long password per account, 15 characters or more where there is no second factor; at least 12 elsewhere (onlinesicherheit.gv.at; NIST sets 8 as the floor with MFA); no forced rotation; change on suspicion; no shared logins.
      - listitem: Keep the list of accounts current and test the admin recovery once a year.
      - listitem: Write the three steps down as a one-page sign-in rule and keep a dated note of what was switched on when; this is the evidence a questionnaire asks for.
    - paragraph: "The Security Evidence Toolkit turns these steps and the other measures a customer or insurer asks about into a self-declaration, an action plan and an emergency card: scutoria.com/toolkits/security-evidence."
    - heading "Sources" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem: "NIST Special Publication 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, July 2025, published 1 August 2025, supersedes revision 3: sections 3.1.1.1, 3.1.1.2, 3.2.2, 4.2. pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html and doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63B-4 · retrieved 2026-10-19."
      - listitem: BSI, press release of 31 January 2025, "Passwortwechseln war gestern", and of 30 January 2026, "Der Ändere-dein-Passwort-Tag braucht ein Update"; consumer pages "Sichere Passwörter erstellen", "Umgang mit Passwörtern" and "Zwei-Faktor-Authentisierung" (undated). bsi.bund.de · retrieved 2026-10-19.
      - listitem: "BSI, IT-Grundschutz-Kompendium, edition 2023: ORP.4 Identitäts- und Berechtigungsmanagement (A1, A2, A8, A9, A22, A23); ORP.2 Personal (A2). bsi.bund.de · retrieved 2026-10-19. Edition 2023 is the latest full edition; the BSI is introducing IT-Grundschutz++ (to be checked at bsi.bund.de; heise, \"IT-Grundschutz++\", and SVA, flyer 2026 · retrieved 2026-10-23)."
      - listitem: CISA, fact sheet "Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA", October 2022; news release of 6 June 2022, "More Than a Password" campaign; blog "Walk this way to enable MFA", 5 May 2022. cisa.gov · retrieved 2026-10-19.
      - listitem: Microsoft, Digital Defense Report 2023 (reporting period July 2022 to June 2023); Microsoft Research, "How effective is multifactor authentication at deterring cyberattacks?", May 2023; Microsoft Security Blog, 20 August 2019. microsoft.com · retrieved 2026-10-19.
      - listitem: "ENISA, \"Cybersecurity guide for SMEs: 12 steps to securing your business\", June 2021, and \"Cybersecurity for SMEs: Challenges and Recommendations\", June 2021. enisa.europa.eu · retrieved 2026-10-19."
      - listitem: "Austria: onlinesicherheit.gv.at, \"Passwort-Auswahl\" (9 December 2025), \"Passwort-Umgang\" (6 February 2020), \"Mehrfaktor-Authentifizierung\" (6 October 2020), news on FIDO security keys (19 September 2023); WKO, \"Mehr Sicherheit durch Mehr-Faktor-Authentifizierung\" (12 September 2022), \"Passwörter: Die Schlüssel zu Computer und Internet\" (6 June 2016), WKO Kärnten news of 28 January 2026. retrieved 2026-10-19."
      - listitem: "Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS 2), Art. 21(2). eur-lex.europa.eu · retrieved 2026-10-19. Germany: BSI-Gesetz of 2 December 2025, § 30(2). gesetze-im-internet.de · retrieved 2026-10-19. Austria: NISG 2026, BGBl. I No. 94/2025, § 32(4), in force since 1 October 2026. ris.bka.gv.at · retrieved 2026-10-19."

AI output reaches customers or the public. AI touches decisions about people. First step: Pause AI-supported decisions about people and any emotion recognition until a specialist has assessed them."
    - heading "What you told us" [level=2]
    - term: AI in use
    - definition: Yes, with business accounts the business set up
    - term: Personal data in tools
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: Written rules
    - definition: Yes, a policy or similar
    - term: Briefing
    - definition: Yes, with a record
    - term: Published AI output
    - definition: "Yes"
    - term: Decisions about people
    - definition: Yes, or planned
    - heading "Where you stand" [level=2]
    - text: Business accounts, training on inputs off, tool register
    - generic: Private accounts or unknown data flows.
    - generic: Open
    - text: Written usage policy with the one page to post
    - generic: Exists; check it against the nine areas.
    - generic: Regulated
    - text: Briefing with record (Article 4 AI Act)
    - generic: Record exists; set the next date.
    - generic: Regulated
    - text: Labelling check (Article 50 AI Act)
    - generic: AI output reaches the public; check the three deployer cases.
    - generic: Open
    - text: Decisions about people kept out
    - generic: High-risk use or prohibited practice to assess.
    - generic: Open
    - heading "Findings" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: AI systems for the recruitment or selection of persons, for decisions on promotion or termination, for task allocation based on behaviour or traits, and for monitoring and evaluating performance are high-risk under Annex III, point 4. The obligations for Annex III high-risk systems apply from 2 December 2027, moved from August 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Since 2 February 2025 the use of AI systems to infer the emotions of a natural person in the workplace is prohibited, except for medical or safety reasons.
    - generic: → Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex III, point 4, Art. 5(1), point (f), Art. 113, points (a) and (c), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 · retrieved 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-19
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: The German data protection authorities advise that employees should not have to work with private accounts, because profiles of individual employees can arise; that accounts should be set at commissioning so that no inputs are used for training and no input history is kept beyond the session; that clear internal instructions should be issued and documented on whether, under which conditions and for which purposes AI applications may be used; and that removing names and addresses is regularly not enough to avoid personal data, because the connection to a person can be restored from the context.
    - generic: → German data protection conference (DSK), Orientierungshilfe "Künstliche Intelligenz und Datenschutz", version 1.0 of 6 May 2024, sections 2.2, 2.4, 2.5 and 3.1 · retrieved 2026-10-18
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: Where a provider processes personal data on behalf of the business, the business may use only processors providing sufficient guarantees, and the processing is governed by a contract that sets out subject-matter, duration, nature and purpose, the type of data and the obligations of both sides. Controller and processor implement technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk.
    - generic: → Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Art. 24(1), Art. 28(1) and (3), Art. 32(1), consolidated version of 4 May 2016 · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-19
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: Article 4(1) of the AI Act asks providers and deployers to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and of other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their knowledge, experience, education and the context of use; it does not require guaranteeing any specific level for any individual. The article has applied since 2 February 2025. The Commission writes that no certificate is needed and that organisations can keep an internal record of trainings.
    - generic: → Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 4(1) and Art. 113, point (a), consolidated version of 27 July 2026 · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-19; European Commission, AI literacy, questions and answers, page dated 27 July 2026 · retrieved 2026-10-18
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Interpretation
      - text: Neither the AI Act nor the GDPR contains a provision that explicitly requires a written AI usage policy. Article 4 asks for measures that support literacy, Article 24(1) GDPR asks the controller for technical and organisational measures that are reviewed and updated, and the Trade Secrets Directive protects information only if reasonable steps were taken to keep it secret. A policy is the usual way to meet all three at once, not a duty of its own.
    - generic: → Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 4; Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Art. 24(1); Directive (EU) 2016/943, Art. 2(1), point (c) · retrieved 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-19
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Fact
      - text: "Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. For a business that uses tools made by others, three cases matter: emotion recognition or biometric categorisation (information of the persons exposed), real-looking AI images, audio or video (disclosure as artificially generated), and AI text published to inform the public on matters of public interest (label, unless a documented human review and a named editorial responsibility exist). Internal use and individual correspondence are not published in the sense of the Commission's guidelines."
    - generic: → Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 50(3) and (4), Art. 113 · retrieved 2026-10-19; Guidelines, annex to C(2026) 5054 final, content approved on 20 July 2026, point 131 · retrieved 2026-10-23
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Gap
      - text: How often a briefing is repeated and how long its record is kept is stated in no source we read. A new or changed tool is an obvious occasion to repeat; the business sets the rhythm.
    - paragraph:
      - generic: Uncertain
      - text: Which authority supervises Articles 4 and 50 is national law. Germany has named the Federal Network Agency (Act of 22 July 2026, in force since 29 July 2026). For Austria, as of 19 October 2026, no official source names the market surveillance authority; the duties apply regardless.
    - generic: → KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsförderungsgesetz of 22 July 2026, BGBl. 2026 I No. 223, § 2(1) · gesetze-im-internet.de · retrieved 2026-10-19; Datenschutzbehörde (Austria), page on artificial intelligence and data protection · dsb.gv.at · retrieved 2026-10-19
    - heading "What to do next" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem: Pause AI-supported decisions about people and emotion recognition; have a specialist assess them against Annex III and Article 5(1)(f) before any restart.
      - listitem: Business accounts for approved tools, training on inputs switched off, one row per tool in a register with the seven approval questions; no private accounts for work.
      - listitem: Check the existing policy against the nine areas and date the current version.
      - listitem: Set the date of the next briefing and brief every new tool.
      - listitem: Run the labelling check under Article 50 for every chatbot, every real-looking image, audio or video and every published text; record the result per case.
      - listitem: "Freeze an evidence page with the date: what is regulated, what is open, who is responsible, when it is reviewed next."
    - paragraph: "The AI Policy Toolkit produces the documents for every step of this plan: the usage policy, the one page to post, the tool register with approval form, the briefing record, the labelling checklist, the enactment plan and the evidence summary, from thirty-four questions, 29 of them required, with a handbook that marks every statement."
    - heading "Sources" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem: "Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024 (AI Act), consolidated version of 27 July 2026: Art. 4, Art. 5(1)(f), Art. 26(2), Art. 50, Art. 113, Annex III point 4. eur-lex.europa.eu · retrieved 2026-10-19."
      - listitem: "Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (Digital Omnibus on AI), in force since 27 July 2026: Art. 1, points (5), (39) and (40). eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj · retrieved 2026-10-18."

      - listitem: "European Commission, Guidelines on the transparency obligations under Article 50, content approved on 20 July 2026 (C(2026) 5054 final, annex), point 131. digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu · retrieved 2026-10-23. To be checked: formal adoption in all languages. Guidance, not law."
